docs.title: Welcome to the ELT Pipeline Engineering Portal
docs.text: This documentation portal captures the architectural principles, configuration guides, data modeling practices, and operations for our Production-Grade ELT Data Pipeline built with Snowflake, dbt Core, and Apache Airflow.

docs.title: 🎯 Project Objective
docs.text:
To build, test, and orchestrate an enterprise-grade ELT pipeline that transforms raw relational data into clean, business-ready dimensional marts while adhering to modern data engineering best practices:

  1. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Principle of least privilege within Snowflake.
  2. Modular Transformations: Staging, Intermediate, Facts, and Marts using dbt Core.
  3. Data Quality Automation: Out-of-the-box schema assertions and custom singular SQL tests.
  4. Cloud-Native Orchestration: Astronomer Cosmos integrating dbt graph lineage dynamically inside Apache Airflow.
  5. Reproducible Infrastructure: Containerized runtime using Docker and OrbStack on Apple Silicon macOS.

docs.title: Dimensional Modeling: Kimball Methodology
docs.text: Dimensional modeling is a database design technique pioneered by Ralph Kimball aimed at optimizing databases for analytics, reporting, and BI readability.

docs.title: 🏛️ Star Schema Architecture
docs.text:
In dimensional modeling, business processes are represented through Facts and Dimensions arranged in a Star Schema:

erDiagram
    DIM_CUSTOMERS ||--o{ FCT_ORDERS : "places"
    DIM_PARTS ||--o{ FCT_ORDER_ITEMS : "contains"
    FCT_ORDERS ||--|{ FCT_ORDER_ITEMS : "includes"
    DIM_SUPPLIERS ||--o{ FCT_ORDER_ITEMS : "supplies"

    DIM_CUSTOMERS {
        int customer_key PK
        string customer_name
        string market_segment
        string nation_name
    }

    FCT_ORDERS {
        int order_key PK
        int customer_key FK
        date order_date
        string order_status
        float total_price
    }

    FCT_ORDER_ITEMS {
        int order_item_key PK
        int order_key FK
        int part_key FK
        int supplier_key FK
        float quantity
        float extended_price
        float discount_amount
        float net_item_sales_amount
    }

docs.title: 1. Fact Tables
docs.text:
• What they represent: Numeric measurements, metrics, and business events (e.g., an order placed, a transaction processed, an item shipped).
  • Characteristics: High row volume, deep table, primarily composed of foreign keys linking to dimensions and numerical additive metrics (e.g., gross_item_sales_amount, tax_amount).
  • Grain: The fundamental level of detail represented by a single row (e.g., one row per line item on an order).

docs.title: 2. Dimension Tables
docs.text:
• What they represent: Contextual attributes that answer the "who, what, where, when, and why" of business events.
  • Characteristics: Wide table with many descriptive text columns (e.g., customer segment, nation, supplier address).
  • Surrogate Keys vs Natural Keys: Natural keys (e.g., CUST_ID) come from source systems; surrogate keys are generated unique integers/hashes to maintain consistency across system changes.

docs.title: 🏗️ dbt Modeling Layers
docs.text:
Our dbt project organizes dimensional models into structured layers:

  1. Sources: Direct pointers to raw Snowflake tables (SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF1).
  2. Staging (stg_): 1-to-1 view wrappers on raw sources; cleans column names, casts datatypes, and trims whitespace.
  3. Intermediate (int_): Joins and complex business calculations between staging models.
  4. Marts (fct_, dim_): Business-facing fact and dimension tables ready for BI visualization.

docs.title: ELT vs ETL: Architectural Paradigms
docs.text: Data engineering pipelines broadly fall into two main architectural patterns: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) and ELT (Extract, Load, Transform).

docs.title: 🔄 Architectural Comparison
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph ETL["Traditional ETL Pattern"]
        direction LR
        S1["Source Systems"] --> E1["Extract"]
        E1 --> T1["Transform Engine<br/>(In-Memory / Middle Tier Server)"]
        T1 --> L1["Load to DWH<br/>(Target Storage)"]
    end

    subgraph ELT["Modern ELT Pattern"]
        direction LR
        S2["Source Systems"] --> E2["Extract"]
        E2 --> L2["Load Raw Data<br/>(Snowflake / BigQuery / Databricks)"]
        L2 --> T2["Transform In-Warehouse<br/>(dbt SQL pushdown)"]
    end

docs.title: ⚖️ Key Differences
docs.text: Dimension Traditional ETL Modern ELT (Our Stack) Transformation Location Dedicated processing server (e.g. Informatica, SSIS, Spark) Inside the Cloud Data Warehouse (Snowflake) Compute Scalability Bound by the middle-tier processing cluster Virtually unlimited on-demand elastic compute Raw Data Availability Raw data is discarded; only transformed tables are stored Raw data is preserved indefinitely in raw/bronze schemas Agility & Changes Schema changes require modifying extraction code and re-ingesting Changing transformations is as simple as updating a dbt SQL query Skill Requirements Proprietary GUI tools or heavy Java/Scala code Standard SQL with Jinja templating

docs.title: 🚀 Why ELT Wins in Modern Cloud Data Warehousing
docs.text:
1. Storage is cheap, compute is elastic: Cloud platforms like Snowflake decouple compute from storage. You can store petabytes of raw data at low cost and spin up compute clusters only when transformations execute.
  2. dbt Pushdown Optimization: dbt does not move data out of Snowflake. Instead, it compiles SQL SELECT statements into DDL/DML (CREATE VIEW AS, CREATE TABLE AS) executed directly inside Snowflake.
  3. Data Democratization: Analysts and analytics engineers write standard SQL rather than depending on specialized data infrastructure engineers for every schema adjustment.

docs.title: Modern Data Stack (MDS)
docs.text: The Modern Data Stack represents the evolution of data infrastructure towards modular, cloud-first, and API-driven tools.

docs.title: 🏗️ Core Layers of the Modern Data Stack
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Ingestion["1. Ingestion / EL<br/>(Airbyte, Fivetran, APIs)"]
    Storage["2. Cloud Storage / Compute<br/>(Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks)"]
    Transform["3. Modeling & Quality<br/>(dbt Core, SQLMesh)"]
    Orchestrate["4. Orchestration<br/>(Apache Airflow, Astronomer, Dagster)"]
    Serve["5. BI & Reverse ETL<br/>(Tableau, PowerBI, Census)"]

    Ingestion --> Storage --> Transform --> Orchestrate --> Serve

docs.title: 🌟 Benefits of the Modern Data Stack
docs.text:
1. Decoupled Architecture: Each component can be upgraded, replaced, or scaled independently without rewriting the entire pipeline.
  2. Software Engineering Best Practices: Version control (Git), automated testing (CI/CD), environment isolation (Dev/Staging/Prod), and code reviews.
  3. Declarative Modeling: You write the desired state of your data models in SQL/YAML; dbt figures out the execution order via directed acyclic graphs (DAGs).

docs.title: Airflow & Astronomer Cosmos Architecture
docs.text: This document describes how Apache Airflow orchestrates dbt models using Astronomer Cosmos.

docs.title: 🚀 Why Astronomer Cosmos?
docs.text:
Traditionally, running dbt in Airflow involved either: 1. Running a monolithic BashOperator(bash_command='dbt run'), which hides model-level lineage and causes entire pipeline reruns on single failures. 2. Manually maintaining hundreds of individual Python operators.

Astronomer Cosmos parses the dbt manifest dynamically and converts each dbt model into an individual Airflow task, giving you: * Native DAG visualization matching your dbt lineage graph. * Granular task retries on failure. * Direct logs per model inside the Airflow UI.

docs.title: Running & Monitoring Airflow DAGs in Docker
docs.text: Instructions for executing and observing orchestrated pipelines via Docker and Astronomer CLI.

docs.title: ⚡ Starting Airflow
docs.text:
From the airflow/ project directory:

cd airflow
astro dev start

This starts: - Airflow Webserver: http://localhost:8080 (Default credentials: admin / admin) - Airflow Scheduler - PostgreSQL metadata database - Airflow Triggerer

docs.text: astro dev stop

docs.title: Marts & Fact Modeling
docs.text: The Marts layer houses business-facing models, including Fact tables and Dimensions designed for analytics reporting.

docs.title: 🏛️ Models Overview
docs.text:
• fct_orders.sql: Captures order-level summaries, pricing metrics, and discount totals.
  • dim_customers.sql: Provides customer demographic and segmentation attributes.
  • monthly_sales_summary.sql: Aggregate reporting mart for executive dashboards.

docs.title: 💾 Materialization Strategy
docs.text: Unlike staging models (views), marts are materialized as table or incremental to ensure fast query response times for BI tools.

docs.title: Staging Layer Models
docs.text: The staging layer acts as the foundational abstraction layer above raw Snowflake sources.

docs.title: 🎯 Purpose of Staging
docs.text:
• Clean Column Names: Convert uppercase or obscure source column names (O_ORDERKEY, C_CUSTKEY) into standard snake_case identifiers (order_key, customer_key).
  • Data Type Casting: Explicitly cast strings, floats, and timestamps.
  • Deduplication & Trimming: Remove whitespace and handle nulls consistently.
  • Lightweight Views: Staging models are materialized as view rather than physical tables to save storage and ensure fresh source reads.

flowchart TD
    SRC["Raw Source: TPCH_SF1"]
    SRC --> STG_O["stg_tpch_orders.sql"]
    SRC --> STG_C["stg_tpch_customers.sql"]

docs.title: Data Quality Testing & Macros
docs.text: Data reliability is maintained through automated generic tests, singular tests, and reusable Jinja macros.

docs.title: 1. Generic Schema Tests (YAML)
docs.text: Defined directly in models/**/*.yml: - unique: Ensures no duplicate primary keys exist. - not_null: Asserts that critical columns have non-null values. - accepted_values: Validates status codes against allowed values (e.g., ['O', 'F', 'P']). - relationships: Enforces foreign key referential integrity between fact and dimension tables.

docs.title: 2. Singular Tests (Custom SQL)
docs.text: Written as standalone SQL queries in the tests/ directory. If the query returns zero rows, the test passes. If rows are returned, the test fails.

docs.title: ⚙️ Jinja Macros
docs.text: Macros are reusable functions written in Jinja/SQL: - Money and pricing calculations (e.g. discounting and tax functions). - Date standardizations and timezone conversions.

docs.title: 1. Conda Environment (elt_env)
docs.text:
We run an isolated Python 3.11 environment to ensure package stability and avoid system library collisions:

# Create environment
conda create -n elt_env python=3.11 -y

# Activate environment
conda activate elt_env

# Install dbt with Snowflake adapter
pip install dbt-snowflake

docs.title: 2. OrbStack (Docker Engine)
docs.text:
We use OrbStack for container management: * Speed: Starts in under 2 seconds. * Low Resource Usage: Uses up to 80% less memory and CPU than Docker Desktop. * CLI Native: Native drop-in for docker and docker compose.

Commands to verify: 

docker --version
docker ps

Astronomer CLI manages local Apache Airflow containers tailored for data engineering:

Open http://localhost:8000 in your browser.

docs.title: Snowflake Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) & DWH Setup
docs.text: In this section, we set up an isolated, secure environment inside Snowflake adhering to the Principle of Least Privilege.

docs.title: 🔐 Architecture Principles
docs.text:
1. Never use ACCOUNTADMIN for automated pipelines: Administrative roles have unrestricted access and can cause accidental data loss or security breaches.
  2. Dedicated Virtual Warehouse: Isolated compute prevents long-running data transformations from blocking ad-hoc analytics or BI queries.
  3. Auto-Suspend & Auto-Resume: Set warehouse auto-suspend to 60 seconds to minimize credit consumption during idle periods.
  4. Imported Privileges on Sample Data: dbt requires read-only permissions on the raw source dataset (SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA).

docs.title: 🛠️ Snowflake Worksheet Setup Script
docs.text:
Open your Snowflake Web Console, navigate to Worksheets, and execute the following SQL script as ACCOUNTADMIN:

-- 1. Use high-privileged role to provision infrastructure
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

-- 2. Create dedicated virtual warehouse for dbt transformations
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS TRANSFORM_WH
    WITH 
    WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
    AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
    AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
    INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE
    COMMENT = 'Virtual warehouse for dbt and Airflow transformations';

-- 3. Create target transformation database
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS DEMO_DWH
    COMMENT = 'Destination analytics warehouse for dbt models';

-- 4. Create development schemas
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS DEMO_DWH.DEV_STAGING;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS DEMO_DWH.DEV_MARTS;

-- 5. Create transformation role
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS DBT_ROLE
    COMMENT = 'Service role for dbt and Airflow ELT pipeline';

-- 6. Grant warehouse permissions
GRANT USAGE, OPERATE ON WAREHOUSE TRANSFORM_WH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;

-- 7. Grant database and schema privileges
GRANT USAGE, CREATE SCHEMA ON DATABASE DEMO_DWH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON ALL SCHEMAS IN DATABASE DEMO_DWH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON FUTURE SCHEMAS IN DATABASE DEMO_DWH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON ALL TABLES IN DATABASE DEMO_DWH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON FUTURE TABLES IN DATABASE DEMO_DWH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON ALL VIEWS IN DATABASE DEMO_DWH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON FUTURE VIEWS IN DATABASE DEMO_DWH TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;

-- 8. Grant read-only access to TPC-H sample data
GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA TO ROLE DBT_ROLE;

-- 9. Create dedicated service user for dbt / Airflow
-- NOTE: Replace 'YourStrongPassword123!' with your chosen password
CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS DBT_USER
    PASSWORD = 'YourStrongPassword123!'
    DEFAULT_ROLE = 'DBT_ROLE'
    DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = 'TRANSFORM_WH'
    DEFAULT_NAMESPACE = 'DEMO_DWH.DEV_STAGING'
    MUST_CHANGE_PASSWORD = FALSE
    COMMENT = 'Service account for dbt and Airflow automation';

-- 10. Assign role to user
GRANT ROLE DBT_ROLE TO USER DBT_USER;

-- 11. Grant role to your current login user and sysadmin for UI visibility
GRANT ROLE DBT_ROLE TO ROLE SYSADMIN;

docs.title: Data Engineering & AI Engineering: Architecture, Tooling, and Frameworks
docs.text: This guide provides a comprehensive reference mapping the tools, frameworks, environments, and libraries across data engineering stages for both AI & Generative AI Systems and Enterprise IT / Lakehouse Architectures.

docs.title: 1. Architectural Foundations: ETL vs. ELT
docs.text:
ETL (Traditional)
[ Sources ] ──> [ Extract ] ──> [ Transform (Spark / Airflow) ] ──> [ Load into DWH ]

ELT (Modern Cloud)
[ Sources ] ──> [ Extract ] ──> [ Load (Object Storage / Lake) ] ──> [ Transform inside Warehouse / Lakehouse ]
Dimension ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) Compute Engine Dedicated external compute engine (Informatica, Talend, custom Spark cluster). Cloud Data Platform (Snowflake Virtual Warehouses, Databricks Spark/Photon, BigQuery). Storage Strategy Only transformed / modeled data reaches the final analytical warehouse. Raw data lands immediately in object storage or data tables. Flexibility Rigid. Schema changes require modifying extraction & transformation code. High. Raw data is preserved, allowing re-processing and retrospective queries. Speed to Ingest Slower (bottlenecked by transformation stage). Rapid (bulk ingestion happens first). Compliance / Privacy Anonymization/masking happens before landing in storage. Masking/RBAC/governance applied at transformation or via row/column policies. Modern Stack Spark, PySpark, Airflow (orchestration). Fivetran/Airbyte (Extract/Load) + dbt/SQL/Spark (Transform).

docs.title: 2. Modern Cloud Platforms: Snowflake vs. Databricks
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      dbt / SQL / BI                    │
└───────────────┬────────────────────────┬───────────────┘
                │                        │
       ┌────────▼────────┐      ┌────────▼────────┐
       │    Snowflake    │      │   Databricks    │
       │ Virtual Whs     │      │ Apache Spark    │
       │ Dynamic Tables  │      │ Delta Live Tabs │
       │ Snowpark        │      │ Unity Catalog   │
       └────────┬────────┘      └────────┬────────┘
                │                        │
       ┌────────▼────────────────────────▼────────┐
       │   Cloud Object Storage (S3 / GCS / Azure)│
       │          Open Formats (Delta / Iceberg)  │
       └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
Feature Snowflake Databricks Core Heritage Cloud-native Data Warehouse (SaaS, SQL-first). Managed Apache Spark / Lakehouse (code-first, Python/Scala). Architecture Separated storage and multi-cluster shared compute (Virtual Warehouses). Lakehouse architecture using Delta Lake format on your cloud storage buckets. Transformation Paradigm SQL, Dynamic Tables, Streams & Tasks, Snowpark (Python/DataFrames). Spark SQL, PySpark, Delta Live Tables (DLT). Open Formats Proprietary micro-partitions, full read/write support for Apache Iceberg. Delta Lake (Linux Foundation open source standard). Data Governance Horizon Catalog (built-in tags, masking policies, row access policies). Unity Catalog (centralized governance across data, AI models, and files). Best Suited For Enterprise analytics, SQL reporting, BI dashboards, low operational overhead. Heavy transformations, machine learning, unstructured data, complex streaming, end-to-end AI/ML.

docs.title: 3. The Medallion Architecture (Bronze → Silver → Gold)
docs.text:
[ Raw Sources ]
       │ (APIs, Databases, Event Streams)
       ▼
┌──────────────────┐
│   BRONZE LAYER   │  Raw, append-only ingestion with source metadata
│   (Raw / Staging)│  (timestamps, source origins, raw JSON payloads).
└────────┬─────────┘
         │  Cleaning, deduplication, schema enforcement, filtering
         ▼
┌──────────────────┐
│   SILVER LAYER   │  Enriched, cleaned, standardized enterprise data model
│   (Cleansed)     │  (conformed dimensions, parsed customer details, valid records).
└────────┬─────────┘
         │  Aggregations, business metrics, star schemas (Fact / Dimension)
         ▼
┌──────────────────┐
│    GOLD LAYER    │  Consumption-ready data for BI, reporting,
│   (Curated)      │  ML feature stores, and RAG retrieval indexes.
└──────────────────┘

docs.title: AI Pipeline Stage Breakdown
docs.text: Stage Key Objective Primary Technologies 1. Parsing & Extraction Convert messy PDFs, markdown, HTML, and audio into machine-readable text while keeping metadata intact. Unstructured.io, LlamaParse, PyMuPDF, Playwright, Debezium 2. Processing & Chunking Parallel preprocessing and semantic splitting (fixed-size, markdown-aware, or token-based). Ray, PySpark, Polars, LangChain Splitters, tiktoken 3. Embeddings & Stores Transform clean text tokens into high-dimensional vectors and index them for similarity search. sentence-transformers, Pinecone, Qdrant, pgvector, Feast 4. Serving & Retrieval Expose fast API query endpoints, combine semantic search with BM25 keyword search, and apply reranking. FastAPI, vLLM, Cohere Rerank, LangServe 5. Observability & Guardrails Track token costs, monitor context hallucination, and prevent prompt injection before sending prompts to the LLM. LangSmith, Ragas, NeMo Guardrails, Phoenix

docs.title: 5. Flowchart 2: Data Engineering in the IT Enterprise (Modern Lakehouse & BI)
docs.text:
This pipeline represents the enterprise IT data lifecycle: ingesting relational OLTP databases and SaaS apps, landing them in object storage, structuring them with Medallion architecture, and serving downstream business intelligence.

flowchart TD
    subgraph EStage1["1. Enterprise Sources & Raw Ingestion"]
        subgraph E1_Src["Source Systems"]

docs.title: Enterprise Pipeline Stage Breakdown
docs.text: Stage Key Objective Primary Technologies 1. Enterprise Ingestion Extract transactional records, operational tables, and change feeds with low source disruption. Fivetran, Airbyte, Apache Kafka, Debezium, AWS DMS 2. Storage & Open Formats Persist uncompressed raw files with ACID transaction guarantees, time travel, and unified metadata. AWS S3, ADLS Gen2, Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg 3. Compute, Modeling & Quality Execute SQL/Python transformations to build dimensional models (Star Schemas) with automated test validation. Snowflake, Databricks, dbt, PySpark, Great Expectations 4. Orchestration & DataOps Coordinate dependency graphs (DAGs), automate testing with Git version control, and provision infrastructure. Apache Airflow, Dagster, GitHub Actions, Terraform, Docker 5. Governance & BI Serving Centralize role-based access control (RBAC), feed executive dashboards, and push data back into operational tools (CRMs). Power BI, Tableau, Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon, Census

docs.title: 6. Enterprise IT vs. AI Data Engineering Comparison
docs.text: Dimension Enterprise IT Data Engineering AI & GenAI Data Engineering Primary Data Type Structured / Tabular (Relational, JSON) Unstructured (Text, PDFs, Audio, Images) Core Compute Task SQL joins, aggregations, schema mapping Chunking, tokenization, vector inference Primary Target Store Data Warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery) Vector DBs (Qdrant, Pinecone, pgvector) SLA & Freshness Batch (hourly/daily) or Micro-batch Real-time semantic retrieval (<100ms) Serving Layer SQL, BI Dashboards (Power BI, Tableau) REST APIs (FastAPI) & LLM context windows

docs.title: 7. FastAPI Production Pattern for Data & AI Retrieval
docs.text:
Minimal Production-Grade Pattern: Vector Search Service

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, status
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import List
import time

app = FastAPI(
    title="Data & Retrieval Service",
    description="Vector search & data serving endpoint for LLM/RAG pipelines",
    version="1.0.0"
)

# 1. Pydantic Request Model with Schema Validation
class SearchQuery(BaseModel):
    query_text: str = Field(..., min_length=3, description="User search query")
    top_k: int = Field(default=5, ge=1, le=50, description="Number of results to retrieve")
    filter_source: str | None = Field(default=None, description="Optional metadata filter")

# 2. Response Model
class DocumentChunk(BaseModel):
    chunk_id: str
    content: str
    similarity_score: float
    source: str

class SearchResponse(BaseModel):
    results: List[DocumentChunk]
    execution_time_ms: float

# 3. Healthcheck Endpoint (Essential for K8s / Cloud Deployments)
@app.get("/healthz", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)
def health_check():
    return {"status": "healthy", "timestamp": time.time()}

# 4. Search Retrieval Endpoint
@app.post("/v1/retrieve", response_model=SearchResponse)
async def retrieve_context(payload: SearchQuery):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        # Connect to Vector DB (Pinecone / Milvus / pgvector)
        mock_results = [
            DocumentChunk(
                chunk_id="doc_101_chunk_3",
                content="Snowflake handles dynamic tables through declarative SQL pipelines.",
                similarity_score=0.91,
                source="snowflake_docs"
            )
        ]
        duration = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        return SearchResponse(results=mock_results, execution_time_ms=round(duration, 2))
    except Exception as exc:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
            detail=f"Retrieval failed: {str(exc)}"
        )

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
Before any code, keep this model in your head:

 Snowflake sample data  ──►  dbt (transform inside Snowflake)  ──►  Airflow (runs dbt on a schedule)
   [Extract + Load:            staging → intermediate → fact         [Orchestration]
    already done for you]      + tests + macros
  • ELT, not ETL. The data is loaded into the warehouse raw, and the transformation happens inside the warehouse using SQL. dbt never moves data. It only sends SQL to Snowflake, and Snowflake does the work.
  • The video skips the "E" and "L" by using Snowflake's built-in TPC-H sample dataset (SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF1), a fake business with customers, orders and line items. That lets you focus on the "T".

docs.title: Lesson 1: Setting Up Snowflake and dbt
docs.text:
Video: 1:35–7:52

What happens: Jay runs a SQL worksheet in Snowflake, then runs dbt init in the terminal.

use role accountadmin;

create warehouse dbt_wh with warehouse_size='x-small';
create database if not exists dbt_db;
create role if not exists dbt_role;

grant role dbt_role to user <your_user>;
grant usage on warehouse dbt_wh to role dbt_role;
grant all on database dbt_db to role dbt_role;

use role dbt_role;
create schema if not exists dbt_db.dbt_schema;

docs.title: Concepts to learn
docs.text:
Snowflake object What it is Analogy Warehouse (dbt_wh) Compute that runs queries and is billed while running The engine Database / schema (dbt_db.dbt_schema) Storage, a container for tables and views The garage Role (dbt_role) A bundle of permissions A key card
  1. Compute and storage are separate. You can resize or pause the warehouse without touching the data. x-small is the cheapest size, which is plenty for learning.
  2. RBAC (role-based access control). Permissions are granted to roles, and roles are granted to users.
    • grant usage on warehouse lets the role run queries on that compute.
    • grant all on database lets the role create schemas and tables there.
    • grant role ... to user lets you act as that role.
  3. Least privilege. dbt runs as dbt_role, not accountadmin. A mistake in dbt then can't drop the whole account.
  4. Two dbt config files people often confuse:
    • ~/.dbt/profiles.yml holds how to connect: account, user, password, role, warehouse. It stays on your machine and is never committed.
    • dbt_project.yml holds how to build the project. It lives in the repo and is shared.

Check yourself

  • Q1. If you run drop warehouse dbt_wh, is any data lost?
  • Q2. Why grant permissions to a role instead of directly to the user?

docs.title: Lesson 2: dbt Project Config and Packages
docs.text:
Video: 7:52–11:45

What happens: Jay deletes the example models, sets materializations per folder, and adds the dbt_utils package.

# dbt_project.yml
models:
  snowflake_workshop:
    staging:
      materialized: view
      snowflake_warehouse: dbt_wh
    marts:
      materialized: table
      snowflake_warehouse: dbt_wh

# packages.yml
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: 1.1.1

Then run dbt deps.

The Notion page labels the first block "dbt_profile.yaml", but it belongs in dbt_project.yml. It also leaves out packages.yml, which the next lesson needs.

docs.title: Concepts to learn
docs.text:
1. Materialization is what dbt creates in Snowflake from your SELECT.
    • view is just saved SQL. It is cheap to build and always fresh, but it recomputes every time someone queries it.
    • table stores the results physically. Queries against it are fast, but you have to rebuild it to refresh it.
  2. Why staging uses views and marts use tables. Staging models are light renames that only feed other models. Marts are what analysts and BI tools query heavily, so they are worth storing.
  3. Folder-level config. Setting staging: materialized: view once applies to every model in that folder. It is the same idea as the DRY macro in Lesson 4, applied to config.
  4. Packages. packages.yml plus dbt deps works like pip install for dbt. dbt_utils is the most common package, and you'll use its generate_surrogate_key macro next.

Check yourself

  • Q3. A model is queried 500 times a day by a dashboard. Should it be a view or a table, and why?

docs.title: Lesson 3: Sources and Staging Models
docs.text:
Video: 11:45–17:41

What happens: Jay writes tpch_sources.yml, stg_tpch_orders.sql and stg_tpch_line_items.sql.

# models/staging/tpch_sources.yml
version: 2

sources:
  - name: tpch
    database: snowflake_sample_data
    schema: tpch_sf1
    tables:
      - name: orders
        columns:
          - name: o_orderkey
            tests:
              - unique
              - not_null
      - name: lineitem
        columns:
          - name: l_orderkey
            tests:
              - relationships:
                  to: source('tpch', 'orders')
                  field: o_orderkey

-- models/staging/stg_tpch_line_items.sql
select
    {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['l_orderkey', 'l_linenumber']) }} as order_item_key,
    l_orderkey as order_key,
    l_partkey as part_key,
    l_linenumber as line_number,
    l_quantity as quantity,
    l_extendedprice as extended_price,
    l_discount as discount_percentage,
    l_tax as tax_rate
from {{ source('tpch', 'lineitem') }}

docs.title: Concepts to learn
docs.text:
1. source() vs a hard-coded table name. Writing {{ source('tpch','orders') }} instead of snowflake_sample_data.tpch_sf1.orders has three benefits:
    • dbt knows the raw input, so it appears in the lineage graph (dbt docs generate).
    • You can change the database or schema in one YAML file.
    • You can attach tests to raw data before you build anything on it.
  2. What the staging layer is for. It mirrors the source one-to-one and cleans it up: renames columns (o_custkey → customer_key) and does light casts, with no joins and no business logic. Every later model reads from staging and never from the raw tables.
  3. Grain and surrogate keys. This is the most important modeling idea in the video.
    • Grain means "what does one row represent?" In orders, one row is one order. In lineitem, one row is one item within an order.
    • l_orderkey alone is not unique in line items, because one order has many items. The unique combination is (l_orderkey, l_linenumber).
    • generate_surrogate_key([...]) hashes those columns into a single unique ID, order_item_key, which makes joins and tests simple.
  4. Source tests. unique and not_null on o_orderkey check the primary key. relationships checks that every line item points to an order that actually exists, which is a foreign-key check.

Try it: run dbt run -s stg_tpch_orders, then look for the view in Snowflake under dbt_db.dbt_schema.

Check yourself

  • Q4. Why would a unique test on l_orderkey fail?

docs.title: Lesson 4: Transformed Models and Macros
docs.text:
Video: 17:41–24:23 (macros start at 20:25)

What happens: Jay builds int_order_items, writes the discounted_amount macro, then builds int_order_items_summary and fct_orders. The chapter order (models at 17:41, macros at 20:25) suggests he writes the join first and then pulls the discount math out into a macro.

-- macros/pricing.sql
{% macro discounted_amount(extended_price, discount_percentage, scale=2) %}
    (-1 * {{extended_price}} * {{discount_percentage}})::decimal(16, {{ scale }})
{% endmacro %}

-- models/marts/int_order_items_summary.sql
select
    order_key,
    sum(extended_price) as gross_item_sales_amount,
    sum(item_discount_amount) as item_discount_amount
from {{ ref('int_order_items') }}
group by order_key

docs.title: Concepts to learn
docs.text:
1. The layered flow:

    stg_tpch_orders ─────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                     ├─► int_order_items ─► int_order_items_summary ─┴─► fct_orders
stg_tpch_line_items ─┘   (grain: item)      (grain: order)               (grain: order)
    • Intermediate models do joins and calculations, and they can change the grain. Here, the summary goes from item level to order level with group by order_key.
    • Fact table (fct_): one row per business event (an order) with numeric measures (sales, discount) and keys to dimensions (customer_key).
    • A data mart is the set of final, business-ready tables for one area, such as sales.

  2. ref() builds the DAG. {{ ref('stg_tpch_orders') }} resolves to the real table name and tells dbt the dependency. You never set the run order yourself. dbt works it out, and this is what lets Airflow draw the graph in Lesson 6.

  3. Why aggregate before joining. Joining orders directly to line items gives many rows per order. Summarizing to one row per order first means fct_orders keeps the same grain as orders, so the numbers aren't inflated.
  4. Macros, Jinja and DRY. A macro is a reusable SQL snippet with parameters. If the discount formula appears in five models and the business changes it, you edit one file. Open target/compiled/... to see the plain SQL that dbt actually sends to Snowflake. This is the best way to understand Jinja.
  5. A detail to notice: the macro returns a negative number (-1 * price * discount). That is a deliberate convention, discounts as negative money, and Lesson 5 tests it.

Check yourself

  • Q5. What would go wrong if fct_orders joined stg_tpch_line_items directly instead of the summary?
  • Q6. You never told dbt to build int_order_items before fct_orders. How did it know?

docs.title: Lesson 5: Generic and Singular Tests
docs.text:
Video: 24:23–29:35

What happens: Jay writes generic_tests.yml plus two SQL test files, then runs dbt test.

# models/marts/generic_tests.yml
models:
  - name: fct_orders
    columns:
      - name: order_key
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('stg_tpch_orders')
              field: order_key
              severity: warn
      - name: status_code
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['P', 'O', 'F']

-- tests/fct_orders_date_valid.sql
select *
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
where date(order_date) > current_date()
   or date(order_date) < date('1990-01-01')

docs.title: Concepts to learn
docs.text:
1. How every dbt test works: a test is a query that returns the bad rows. Zero rows means pass, and any rows means fail.
  2. Generic tests are reusable and declared in YAML: unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values. The accepted_values: ['P','O','F'] test catches new or unexpected status codes coming from upstream.
  3. Singular tests are one-off SQL files in tests/ for business rules. In this project:
    • fct_orders_discount.sql: discounts must not be positive (this is why the macro returns negative values).
    • fct_orders_date_valid.sql: order dates must not be in the future or before 1990.
  4. severity: warn reports the problem without failing the run. Use it for checks that are worth knowing about but shouldn't block the pipeline.
  5. dbt build runs models and tests in DAG order, so a failing test stops the models downstream of it. That is what you want in production.

Check yourself

  • Q7. Write a singular test asserting that gross_item_sales_amount is never negative.

docs.title: Lesson 6: Deploying with Airflow
docs.text:
Video: 29:35–end

What happens: Jay creates an Astronomer project, installs dbt in a virtual environment inside the Docker image, adds a Snowflake connection in the Airflow UI, writes dbt_dag.py, and triggers it.

brew install astro
mkdir dbt-dag && cd dbt-dag
astro dev init
# copy the dbt project to dags/dbt/data_pipeline/
astro dev start   # UI at http://localhost:8080 (admin / admin)

# Dockerfile (added line)
RUN python -m venv dbt_venv && source dbt_venv/bin/activate && \
    pip install --no-cache-dir dbt-snowflake && deactivate

# requirements.txt
astronomer-cosmos
apache-airflow-providers-snowflake

# dags/dbt_dag.py
import os
from datetime import datetime

from cosmos import DbtDag, ProjectConfig, ProfileConfig, ExecutionConfig
from cosmos.profiles import SnowflakeUserPasswordProfileMapping

profile_config = ProfileConfig(
    profile_name="default",
    target_name="dev",
    profile_mapping=SnowflakeUserPasswordProfileMapping(
        conn_id="snowflake_conn",
        profile_args={"database": "dbt_db", "schema": "dbt_schema"},
    ),
)

dbt_snowflake_dag = DbtDag(
    project_config=ProjectConfig("/usr/local/airflow/dags/dbt/data_pipeline"),
    operator_args={"install_deps": True},
    profile_config=profile_config,
    execution_config=ExecutionConfig(
        dbt_executable_path=f"{os.environ['AIRFLOW_HOME']}/dbt_venv/bin/dbt",
    ),
    schedule_interval="@daily",   # use schedule="@daily" on Airflow 2.4+ / 3
    start_date=datetime(2023, 9, 10),
    catchup=False,
    dag_id="dbt_dag",
)

docs.title: Concepts to learn
docs.text:
1. Why orchestrate? dbt run on your laptop isn't a pipeline. Airflow adds scheduling (@daily), retries, alerting, logs, and a place to put dbt alongside ingestion jobs.
  2. Astro CLI. astro dev init and astro dev start run a full Airflow setup locally in Docker (scheduler, webserver and database).
  3. A separate virtual environment for dbt (the Dockerfile step). Airflow and dbt pin conflicting Python packages. Installing dbt in dbt_venv keeps them apart, and Cosmos calls dbt at that path (ExecutionConfig).
  4. Cosmos is the main idea here. Without it, you'd have one Airflow task running dbt build, which is all or nothing. Cosmos reads your dbt project and creates one Airflow task per model, with its tests, in the same DAG that ref() defined. You can see which model failed and retry just that one.
  5. Credentials from an Airflow connection. SnowflakeUserPasswordProfileMapping(conn_id="snowflake_conn") builds profiles.yml at runtime from the Airflow connection (Admin → Connections, type Snowflake). Secrets stay in Airflow, not in your code.
  6. DAG settings:
    • start_date is when the schedule begins.
    • catchup=False stops Airflow from back-filling a run for every day since 2023.
    • install_deps=True runs dbt deps automatically.

Check yourself

  • Q8. What does Cosmos give you that a single BashOperator running dbt build does not?

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. ELT: load raw data, then transform it in the warehouse with SQL.
  2. Snowflake: compute (warehouses) is separate from storage, and access is granted through roles with least privilege.
  3. Layers: source → staging (clean, 1:1) → intermediate (join, aggregate) → fact/mart (business-ready).
  4. Grain: always know what one row means, and use surrogate keys when no single column is unique.
  5. dbt basics: source(), ref() and the DAG, materializations, macros and Jinja, packages.
  6. Testing: tests return bad rows. Generic tests go in YAML, singular tests go in SQL, and severity controls whether a failure blocks the run.
  7. Orchestration: Airflow plus Cosmos turns the dbt DAG into observable, retryable tasks.

docs.title: Gotchas in the Notion code
docs.text:
• stg_tpch_line_items.sql is listed under models/staging/tpch/, but the other staging files are directly in models/staging/. dbt finds models in either place, so pick one location and use it everywhere.
  • Replace the hard-coded grant role dbt_role to user jayzern; with your own username.
  • schedule_interval is deprecated in Airflow 2.4+ and removed in Airflow 3, so use schedule= there.
  • packages.yml is missing from the notes. Add it, otherwise generate_surrogate_key fails.

docs.title: Homework
docs.text:
1. Add a dimension model, dim_customers, built from tpch.customer, and join it to fct_orders on customer_key.
  2. Add a net_item_sales_amount column (gross + discount) using a new macro.
  3. Add source freshness checks to tpch_sources.yml, and find out why they don't make sense on sample data.
  4. Make one test fail on purpose, then watch how Cosmos shows the failure in the Airflow graph.

docs.title: Self-Check Questions
docs.text: # Lesson Question Q1 1 If you run drop warehouse dbt_wh, is any data lost? Q2 1 Why grant permissions to a role instead of directly to the user? Q3 2 A model is queried 500 times a day by a dashboard. Should it be a view or a table, and why? Q4 3 Why would a unique test on l_orderkey fail? Q5 4 What would go wrong if fct_orders joined stg_tpch_line_items directly instead of the summary? Q6 4 You never told dbt to build int_order_items before fct_orders. How did it know? Q7 5 Write a singular test asserting that gross_item_sales_amount is never negative. Q8 6 What does Cosmos give you that a single BashOperator running dbt build does not?
